title: Licensing and Third-Party Assets
keywords: development tools, build systems, and integration
subtopics: Responsible use of copied code and templates
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of licensing and third-party assets and when it is appropriate.
Apply bootstrap's open-source license using the documented Bootstrap 5.3 pattern.
Check license notices and obligations and identify one likely failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study licensing and third-party assets and connect it to a small implementation or review task. The included subtopics preserve the attached Bootstrap curriculum outline.
content.why_it_matters: Licensing and Third-Party Assets is part of a reproducible delivery workflow. Pin versions, keep source files distinct from generated output, confirm licensing and asset paths, and inspect the built artifacts rather than relying only on a development preview.

content_blocks.code: Bootstrap is distributed under the MIT License. Check the exact version license and the license terms of every separately added font, icon set, image, or plugin before redistribution.

content_blocks.title: Version and implementation note
content_blocks.text: Bootstrap is MIT-licensed, but separate icons, fonts, photos, and third-party plugins can have different terms; review each asset license.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating licensing and third-party assets as a visual-only change.
common_mistakes.why: A class or style does not automatically add semantic meaning, application logic, or secure server behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the appropriate HTML semantics and verify the actual interaction.

common_mistakes.problem: Checking only the default viewport or happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Responsive changes and interaction states can reveal issues that are not visible in a single screenshot.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat the task at a narrow and a wide viewport and include keyboard/error state checks where relevant.
